entry.title: New abstract for LLM-JEPA
entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original abstract is fairly good, actually! In the sense that, at least, i understood some what they were trying to convery in the paper (as opposed to some previous papers we’ve read recently). Another benefit is that it’s actually pretty short and to the point. Having said that, i felt that the abstract, and the paper as a whole, has some JEPA-optimistic bias (which i get!). I tried to rewrite it in a somewhat more balanced way.

Yann (et al)’s version:

Large Language Model (LLM) pretraining, finetuning, and evaluation rely on input-space reconstruction and generative capabilities. Yet, it has been observed in vision that embedding-space training objectives, e.g., with Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), are far superior to their input-space counterpart. That mismatch in how training is achieved between language and vision opens up a natural question: can language training methods learn a few tricks from the vision ones? The lack of JEPA-style LLM is a testimony of the challenge in designing such objectives for language. In this work, we propose a first step in that direction where we develop LLM-JEPA, a JEPA based solution for LLMs applicable both to finetuning and pretraining. Thus far, LLM-JEPA is able to outperform the standard LLM training objectives by a significant margin across models, all while being robust to overfiting. Those findings are observed across numerous datasets (NL-RX, GSM8K, Spider, RottenTomatoes) and various models from the Llama3, OpenELM, Gemma2 and Olmo families.

My Version:

Nowadays, State-of-the-art LLMs are pretrained almost exclusively on a single task - autoregressive text prediction. This loss, powerful as it may be, does not explicitly influence the shape of the representation space. JEPA architerctures, which have shown some favorable results in Vision tasks, focus on shaping the representation space of the inputs. This paper aims to bridge the two. To do so, we offer a combined LLM-JEPA loss, along with small changes to transformer architecture and inputs. We show some gains ranging from modest to substantial, in various models and downstream tasks.

Additional thoughts

The title is good, too, in my opinion. I intentionally removed some of the specifications of the implementation. Besides making it easier to read, my thought was that the readers belong to one of two crowds: (i) familiar with JEPA, in which case the combination is easier to imagine and would want to see the details directly, or (ii) unfamiliar with it, in which they need some background which the asbtract shouldn’t supply. In both cases, leaving it less specific felt more natural to me.

entry.title: Papers worth knowing this week
entry.content:
Cosine Misleads: Auxiliary Losses Reshape Vision Language Models, Not Their Latents

XiuYu Zhang, Junfeng Fang, Zhenkai Liang, 2026.

This paper investigates whether improving the alignment between intermediate latent representations and their target visual embeddings actually improves vision-language model (VLM) performance. This directly addresses a concern raised by LLM-JEPA: forcing related representations to align does not necessarily benefit the model's original task and may even hurt its performance. Their findings suggest that auxiliary representation losses may influence performance by modifying the model's shared parameters rather than by improving the representations used for reasoning.

Next-Latent Prediction Transformers Learn Compact World Models

Jayden Teoh, Manan Tomar, Kwangjun Ahn, Edward S. Hu, Tim Pearce, Pratyusha Sharma, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Riashat Islam, Alex Lamb, John Langford, 2026.

This paper introduces NextLat, an auxiliary training objective that encourages Transformers to predict their next hidden state from the current hidden state and the next token. The goal is to encourage the model to maintain compact internal representations that capture information necessary for future predictions, rather than relying entirely on attention over previous tokens. The authors theoretically show that, under ideal conditions, these hidden states become sufficient for predicting future sequences. This presents another approach to incorporating representation learning into a model's loss function, using the prediction of future hidden states rather than aligning representations of semantically related inputs.

entry.title: Critique of LLM-JEPA: LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS MEET JOINT EMBEDDING PREDICTIVE ARCHITECTURES

link.title: Critique of LLM-JEPA: LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS MEET JOINT EMBEDDING PREDICTIVE ARCHITECTURES

entry.content:
Weaknesses

Writing and notation. Apart from grammatical errors, the notation has been incoherent. Specifically, Pred(Enc(TEXT)) implies that Pred operates on a single vector, whereas it actually operates on the whole token sequence.

Figure 3 (right). This figure serves as a supporting evidence to the use of the JEPA loss term. It has several flaws:

  1. The figure is underspecified. What is the value of k? What is the x axis, and what magnitudes of x values are seen in the figure?
  2. The comparison is misleading for k>0. For nonzero k, the baseline is evaluated on tokens which it didn’t train on - recall that the training for NTP does not include the [PRED] token. Therefore the observed loss may reflect an untrained prediction mechanism rather than a deficiency in the representations learned by the baseline model. There’s also a mathematical argument that explains why the values of the loss when k>0 are around 1. Because the embedding of [PRED] is randomly initialized, and never changes during training, the final-layer representation also has certain distribution properties. Assuming ‘random in random out’, when modeling the output embedding is uniformly distributed on the unit sphere, the expected cosine-similarity between this vector and another vector is 0, and the loss 1. NOTE: inspecting the source code reveals that the default is k=0, but it’s unclear how the experiment was run.
  3. Doesn’t rule out the possibility that the baseline exhibits relative positive vs. negative separation. The JEPA loss takes into account only ‘positive’ pairs, and measures the degree to which the embeddings of pair elements are close in the latent space. It doesn’t take into account whether ‘negative’ pairs induce distant embeddings. Hence, we can’t rule out from the figure (or anywhere else in the paper, as far as I know) that the baseline yields high separation in negative pairs, relative to the separation it yields on positive pairs. It could be that during training, the separation on negative pairs only grows while the separation of positive pairs stays put.
  4. Poor task diversity. The evaluation is done over one specific task of regex generation. It’s unclear whether the JEPA loss is required only for this task, and whether other tasks NTP objective better captures the aims of JEPA.

Flaws in to evaluations. They evaluate the models during and after training.

  1. NL-RX-SYNTH (regex). The way a given output is scored against the ground truth is flawed. Recall the task: the input is a natural language description of a regular expression, and the output should be the regular expression described by the input. Given a predicted regular expression, it is compared by string equality to the ground truth regex. There are multiple (infinite…) ways to write regular expressions for the same regular language. Perhaps the baseline model has certain regex styles it learned from the NTP objective, which is wrongly flagged incorrect.
  2. Rotten Tomatoes. A dataset for the binary classification task of determining the sentiment (Bad/Good) of a movie review. (A) to determine whether the prediction is correct, the first generated token should be the ground truth label. There could be FNs in the scores. The two accuracy results between baseline (56.5%) and LLM-JEPA (57.7%) are very close to one another, as well as to random chance (50%). Without error analysis, it’s hard to infer improvement from this result. (B) only accuracy is reported; a confusion matrix could’ve been insightful.

Unclear contribution of different k values. Figure 7 shows benchmarks using different k values. There’s no clear evidence that certain values of k are generally better than others.

  1. In some cases, k=0 gives better/comparable results to larger values. This calls into question the practical benefits of the additional nonlinear processing provided by predictor tokens.
  2. Why is larger k more important on some tasks but not others? Is there a certain task type that most benefits from larger k?
  3. Whether and how the benefits of large k diminish on longer tasks? Where longer means that the input given to the model is larger.

Underspecification of the negative pair attempt. The authors say they tried training using negative samples as well, with the InfoNCE loss, and got worse results. It doesn’t fit with the intuition, and hence should have been expanded upon in detail. Key knowledge missing: 1) how many negative samples per positive sample was used in a single step? 2) what negatives did they choose, and how difficult were they?

How it could have been improved

Figure 3 (right). 1) Label both axes 2) state k value 3) separate it into two graphs one per evaluated loss 4) add evaluation over (hard) negative pairs as well 5) evaluate over multiple datasets with differing characteristics (and come up with a satisfactory definition of ‘characteristics’)

Evaluations: NL-RX-SYNTH. Instead of string equality, compare the predicted and ground truth regular expressions in terms of the languages they capture. There are algorithms that decide whether two regular expressions have the same language.

Evaluations: Rotten tomatoes. (1) Do error analysis. Show that we don’t need to worry about mis-deserializations. (2) provide confusion matrices.

Effects of k. (1) try to understand which tasks demand large/small k, maybe one may characterize them. (2) fix large k, vary evaluation datasets by length (need to keep the same task though), find out the diminishing returns rule.

Verdict

While the paper does propose and test a direction worth pursuing, I wouldn’t accept the paper as is.
entry.summary: Necessity of JEPA-loss via Fig 3 is flawed; effect of different k values unclear

entry.title: The core idea: a shortcut that helps, until it hurts

link.title: The core idea: a shortcut that helps, until it hurts

entry.content:
How the paper shows it

Figure 3 of the paper explains why recall of the old facts collapses and then recovers on its own. It has three panels: the old facts’ hidden states projected on the shared direction, the size of the common shift s during fine-tuning (with and without normalization), and the shared and individual margins of the new facts.

Everything is there, but the reader has to bring Eq. 5 to decode it. The turning point of the story, the moment the shift starts to hurt the new facts, appears only as the individual margin γ̄ind crossing zero in the right panel. And no panel shows what any of this does to the answer of a single fact.

The redesign

A shared shortcut helps new learning but hides old knowledge. Once precise learning takes over, the shortcut becomes harmful, and retracts. Press Watch the story, or jump between the stages.

What did we just see?

Early in training, the model finds a shortcut: boosting all B answers helps it learn new facts, even before it can distinguish their correct answers. But this shared boost also affects old facts, hiding their correct answers without erasing the underlying information.

The key is RMSNorm. As the shared component grows, normalization weakens the fact-specific signals. Initially, this helps by suppressing misleading signals. Later, once the new associations become accurate, the same effect becomes harmful: the shared boost reduces the score difference between correct and incorrect B answers.

Gradient descent therefore pulls the shared component back. As a side effect, the old facts become accessible again, without ever being retrained.

Not everything comes back

The shared shift can retract: it hid the old fact without erasing it. But a second, slower process is not. Small fact-specific changes keep accumulating and gradually erase some old facts for good. The paper calls this erosion, and only this part is truly catastrophic forgetting.

What changed and why

  • Answers instead of hidden-state geometry, so “the model now answers wrong” is visible directly.
  • One purple lift, identical in both rows, so the shared shift reads as a single object that grows and shrinks.
  • A dashed outline for the stored signal, so hidden and erased look different.

The bars are a qualitative schematic of the mechanism, not measured logits. The curve of the shared lift comes from a simulation of the paper’s minimal model (§3.1; d = 128, α = 0.5, one seed); the code is in minimal_model.py.
entry.summary: Why old facts vanish and come back without retraining, in one picture: a shortcut that helps the new facts, until it hurts them.

entry.title: Does the wording of new facts change spurious forgetting? Rerunning Figure 1 with dossier-style biographies

link.title: Does the wording of new facts change spurious forgetting? Rerunning Figure 1 with dossier-style biographies

entry.content:
What I reimplemented

Figure 1 of When Forgetting is not Catastrophic: On the Mechanics of Spurious Forgetting. The figure has two fine-tuning runs from the same pretrained model:

  • C (mixed answers). The new facts take their answers from the answer pools of both old groups. Old-fact recall drops slowly.
  • B′ (concentrated answers). The new facts take their answers only from old group B’s pool. Old group A’s recall collapses early, then comes back partly without any replay. This is the “spurious” part of the title.

The paper explains the collapse with a shared logit shift: fine-tuning pushes all old prompts toward the new answers in the same direction, and the shift can later be undone. That explanation is about answers. It does not say whether the wording of the new text matters. So I added one extra condition:

Question. If the new biographies use different wording from the pretraining biographies, does the collapse change?

That gives four arms, 2 answer pools × 2 wordings. The two shared-template arms recreate Figure 1. The two structural arms are mine and are not in the paper.

The setup

Starting point. The repository’s MLP-free Transformer at pretraining step 16,000. Before fine-tuning it recalls 100% of first answer tokens for both old groups (A and B). The notebook checks for at least 90% before it continues.

Data. Every person has six facts: birth year, birthplace, university, major, employer and work location. For each attribute, old A takes its answers from half X of the value pool and old B from half Y. The new people are the same in all four arms:

  • Concentrated answers come only from Y (B′ in the paper, disjoint in the code).
  • Mixed answers come from X ∪ Y (C in the paper, all_values in the code). In the saved run, the share from old A’s half was 46.6% to 54.8% across attributes.

The two wordings. Take one new person, Ada Morgan Lee, with birth year 1912 and birthplace Paris:

Wording What the model reads during fine-tuning
Shared templates (the paper’s) The birth year of Ada Morgan Lee is recorded as 1912. The birthplace of Ada Morgan Lee is the city of Paris.
Structural (dossier-style, new) The birth year of Ada Morgan Lee. 1912. The birthplace of Ada Morgan Lee. Paris.

Both wordings use the same token IDs for the name and the answer, so they run on the same checkpoint and vocabulary. Within each answer pool, the two wordings have the same people, facts, attribute order, sampler seed and number of times each person is seen. I checked these with asserts. Old and new people share zero exact person–attribute–value triples.

Evaluation. All four arms are tested on the original-style held-out templates, scoring whether the model predicts the first token of the answer (argmax over the full vocabulary). Old A and old B are tested on their own fixed biographies, which never appear in fine-tuning.

Training. Each arm starts from the same parameters with a fresh AdamW state, the same constant learning rate, and runs 1,200 injection steps.

# Notebook §4, run_arm(): inner loop, simplified
for step in range(1, N_STEPS + 1):
    batch = view.get_batch()                       # new biographies only
    state, loss = train_step(state, batch)         # repository loss
    if step in EVAL_STEPS:
        logits_A = fixed_readout(state, old_A)     # first-answer positions
        shift = (logits_A - logits_A0).mean(axis=people)   # shared per-attribute shift
        log(recall(old_A), recall(old_B), recall(new),
            rms_l2(shift),
            recall(logits_A0 + shift),             # "common only"
            recall(logits_A - shift))              # "varying only"

Full code and saved outputs: biography_wording_forgetting.ipynb. It uses the paper’s repository (JAX) for the data, model, checkpoint and training step.

A caveat about the intervention. The dossier entries are on average about 6.6 tokens shorter per biography, and their answers sit about 3.4 tokens earlier. They also have less template variety. So “wording” here means phrasing, template diversity and answer position all changing together.

Results

1. The shared-template arms reproduce Figure 1

Left: final frame of the paper’s companion animation (500 steps). Right: my run (1,200 steps). Blue is concentrated answers, orange is mixed. Solid is shared templates, dashed is structural wording.

Compare the solid lines with the paper first:

  • Concentrated / shared (solid blue) behaves like B′. Old A falls from 100% to 17.7% by step 50, comes back to about 55% around step 200 with no replay, then declines to 31.2%.
  • Mixed / shared (solid orange) behaves like C. Old A declines slowly to 70.9%, with no early dip.
  • Both reach 100% new-fact recall by step 200.

So the qualitative pattern of Figure 1 reproduces. This is one seed, while the paper’s plotting code averages 3 mixed and 5 concentrated runs, so I compare the shape, not the exact values.

2. Wording changes forgetting, in opposite directions

Top row: recall of old A, old B and new facts. Bottom row: size of the shared logit shift on old A, and old A recall when only the shared shift is applied (common only) or removed (varying only).

Arm Old A lowest Old A final Old B final New facts final Peak shared shift
Concentrated / shared 17.7% 31.2% 74.0% 100.0% 115.5
Concentrated / structural 54.4% 54.4% 49.1% 20.0% 136.2
Mixed / shared 70.9% 70.9% 70.5% 100.0% 117.3
Mixed / structural 52.4% 52.4% 51.8% 14.2% 133.7

Final values are at step 1,200. The shift is the root mean square across attributes of the L2 norm of the mean change in old A’s logits.

  • Concentrated answers: dossier wording removes the collapse. The dashed blue line has no early dip; it declines smoothly. Old A ends 23.2 points higher than with shared templates. But old B ends 24.9 points lower. The forgetting moves from A to B instead of disappearing.
  • Mixed answers: dossier wording makes forgetting worse. Old A ends 18.5 points lower and old B 18.7 points lower than with shared templates.
  • New facts: the dossier arms barely transfer. They reach only 20.0% and 14.2% on the original-style prompts. I did not test them on held-out dossier-style prompts, so I cannot tell if they learned less, or learned the facts in a format that does not carry over to the test prompts.

Interestingly, the two dashed lines almost overlap on old A and old B. With dossier wording, where the answers come from matters much less. The difference between B′ and C that the paper emphasizes is mostly a property of the shared-template arms.

3. At matched new-fact recall, the sign flips

Comparing arms at the same step is not fair when one arm learns the new facts five times better. So I also compared them at the same new-fact recall: for each target, I took each arm’s first crossing and interpolated between saved evaluations.

All four arms only overlap between about 0.7% and 14.2% new-fact recall, the ceiling of the weakest arm. At 14.2%:

Answer pool Old A, shared Old A, structural Structural − shared
Concentrated about 32% about 67% +34.9 points
Mixed about 100% about 52% −47.3 points

The effect of wording has opposite signs in the two pools even here. Mixed / shared barely forgets anything at this level, while mixed / structural has already lost half of old A. The range is narrow and early in training, and the matched points come from different steps and different numbers of examples seen.

4. Is the shared logit shift the cause? Only in one arm

The paper’s explanation predicts that a bigger shared shift means more forgetting. Two measurements disagree with that simple version:

  • Representation overlap goes down with dossier wording. Before fine-tuning, the cosine between old A and new vectors at the answer position is about 0.070–0.127 with shared templates and 0.002–0.038 with dossier entries (all 12 pool × attribute pairs drop).
  • But the shared shift goes up. The peak shift is 134–136 for the dossier arms against 116–117 for the shared arms (bottom-left panel above). Yet the concentrated / structural arm, with the largest shift, has no collapse.

The size of the shift does not track the damage; its direction relative to the correct answers does. The two counterfactual readouts show this:

  • Common only (old logits + shared shift): only concentrated / shared dips, to about 71% around step 100. The other three stay near 100%, even though their real recall falls. So in those three arms, forgetting is not caused by the shared shift.
  • Varying only (current logits − shared shift): removing the shift saves much of the early recall in concentrated / shared. In the other arms it changes little.

So the shared-shift explanation fits the arm that the paper studies (concentrated, shared wording). In the other three arms, the forgetting comes from the person-specific part of the change. These readouts are not an additive split of the lost accuracy, because first-token accuracy depends on the argmax of the combined logits.

What I learned

  • Figure 1 reproduces. With shared templates, concentrated answers give the collapse and partial recovery, and mixed answers give slow forgetting, on a single seed of the repository’s model.
  • Spurious forgetting depends on the wording, not only the answers. Dossier-style text removed the concentrated-answer collapse, but moved the damage to old B, and made forgetting worse under mixed answers. Wording and answer pool interact.
  • Less overlap in representation does not mean less forgetting. The dossier wording lowered the old–new cosine everywhere and still increased forgetting in the mixed pool.
  • The shared logit shift explains the collapse, but not all forgetting. Its size is a poor predictor; only in concentrated / shared does applying it alone reproduce a drop.
  • Caveats. One injection seed and one pretrained checkpoint. The wording intervention also changes length, answer position and template variety. The dossier arms were never scored on dossier-style held-out prompts, so their low new-fact recall may be a transfer problem rather than a learning problem. The external-encoder comparison in the notebook was not run.
  • Next steps. Score new facts on both prompt styles in every arm; add paired seeds and a second checkpoint; and build a lighter paraphrase that keeps the answer position and template variety fixed, to find which feature of the wording matters.
entry.summary: Starting from the paper's Figure 1 Transformer, I fine-tuned on the same new facts in two wordings, shared templates and short dossier entries. The wording changed the forgetting curve, but in opposite directions depending on where the answers come from.

entry.title: Papers worth knowing this week
entry.content:
“Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs”

Randall Balestriero and Yann LeCun, 2026.

This paper proves the conjecture that models trained on different modalities converge to the same internal representation of the world. They do so by training and comparing Good-View Text JEPA, Bad-View Text JEPA, standard next-token LLM, and image JPEA. The results show the good-view model aligns with the image model far better than all others. Furthermore, good-view training needs 42x fewer samples than next-token prediction to reach the same cross-modal alignment.

“VL-JEPA: Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture for Vision-language”

Delong Chen, Mustafa Shukor, Theo Moutakanni, Willy Chung, Jade Yu, Tejaswi Kasarla, Yejin Bang, Allen Bolourchi, Yann LeCun, Pascale Fung, 2025.

This paper replaces standard autoregressive text-token generation in vision-language models (VLMs) with a JEPA that predicts continuous embeddings of the target text in latent space. The results show VL-JEPA training requires 50% fewer trainable parameters than the original VLMs.
entry.summary: Two recent and trending papers about JEPA.

entry.title: A better Figure 3
entry.content:
How to read it

Each hidden state is drawn in two dimensions. The horizontal position is the shared direction, which decides whether the old answers or the new answers win. The vertical position is the fact’s own part, which picks its answer within that region. A fact is answered when it sits on its own spot.

The three phases

Before finetuning, the old facts sit on their spots and the new facts are unknown.

In the collapse, the new facts all answer in the same region, so their errors agree and add up to one push that moves every hidden state the same way. The old facts are carried into the wrong region together. Some new facts already reach their spots.

In the recovery, each new fact learns its own part. With normalization the length of every hidden state is fixed, so a long shared shift leaves less room for the own parts. Once the new facts depend on their own parts, the shift is pulled back and most old facts return to their region. Without normalization nothing pulls the shift back, and the old facts stay out.

In the erosion, single old facts drift off their own spots. This slow loss is specific to each fact and is the part of the forgetting that does not come back.

The old facts were never erased. During the collapse they moved as one group and kept their own parts, which is why the recovery needs no replay of old data.
entry.summary: A schematic of the three phases of finetuning, with and without normalization, showing where the old and the new facts land and which ones are answered.

entry.title: Why did OLMo recover old facts in only one experiment?

link.title: Why did OLMo recover old facts in only one experiment?

entry.content:
I think the strongest result comes from the experiment with the small Transformer. After training on new facts, the model starts to favor the same set of answers across many old questions. When the authors remove this shared bias from the answer scores, the model answers most of those questions correctly again. It does this without training on the old facts a second time.

My main concern is why OLMo recovered some old facts in one experiment but not in the other. The authors train two copies of OLMo on different data. One learns facts about fictional people, such as where they work. The other learns who makes real products. Both start making mistakes on old facts. With more training, the first model gets some of those facts right again. The second does not show the same recovery.

The authors suggest that the difference comes from a clue in the new data. A fictional person’s name gives no clue about an employer chosen at random. But if the model recognizes a product as a car, it can narrow down the list of manufacturers. Favoring car companies helps it answer questions about several products, so it has a reason to keep that bias.

I find this explanation plausible, but the experiment changes two things at once: how useful the clue is and how much the model already knows about the subject. For example, the model might recognize a car and know where it is sold without knowing who makes it. Learning its manufacturer adds one fact about a familiar product. A fictional person, on the other hand, is someone the model has never seen before. From these two runs alone, we cannot tell whether recovery depends on the clue, on how familiar the subject is, or on both.

I would test this using the same fictional products and the same four manufacturers in both runs. In the first run, two companies make cameras and the other two make speakers. Knowing the product type narrows the answer down to two companies. In the second run, I would shuffle the assignments so that each company makes cameras and speakers equally often. I would keep the wording, the amount of training, and the number of examples per company the same. If accuracy on old facts recovers more in the second run, that would be stronger evidence that the clue itself affects recovery.

This matters in practice: when a model starts making mistakes on facts it used to know, the paper does not yet show how to tell whether more training will bring those answers back.
entry.summary: A critique of what the two OLMo training runs tell us about recovery and how to test the explanation.
